echoes.note: The opening of the sea-voyage sets up the psalm's tableau of those who 'go down to the sea in ships, that do business in great waters'; here the verbal contact is minimal (mere embarkation and difficult sailing), so the echo is faint and anticipatory, gathering force only when the storm breaks. Thematic coherence is real but volume is near zero at this stage.

Like Jonah, who 'found a ship' and boarded for a sea-passage toward a distant destination, Paul is put aboard ship after ship bound westward; the framing of a divinely-directed man embarking on a fraught Mediterranean voyage primes the Jonah typology that the storm scene activates. Verbal borrowing is slight, so this is a low-confidence narrative resonance.

Luke dates the danger by noting 'the Fast had now already gone by' — the Day of Atonement, whose fixed autumn date (the tenth of the seventh month) Leviticus prescribes as a day of self-affliction. The detail is a calendar marker rather than a theological citation, but it presupposes the Levitical institution and places the voyage in the perilous post-Atonement sailing season.

A second locus for the Day of Atonement 'Fast' that Luke's temporal note assumes; the same calendrical institution underlies the warning that the voyage has become dangerous. Offered as an alternate scriptural anchor for the same allusion.

The closest narrative parallel: a violent wind hurled upon the sea, a ship in danger of breaking, terrified mariners, and the casting of cargo overboard to lighten the vessel — all of which recur here (Euroclydon, reinforcing the hull, jettisoning cargo and tackle). The shared storm-script and the act of throwing freight into the sea give real thematic and motif coherence, though Luke borrows the type, not the words.

The psalm's seafarers meet a 'stormy wind' that lifts the waves, so that 'they reel to and fro, and are at their wits' end' — answering precisely to the driven, rudderless ship and the loss of all hope of being saved. The progression from tempest to despair tracks the psalm's movement and is the chapter's strongest figural backbone for the storm.

Ezekiel's dirge over Tyre depicts the merchant ship driven into the heart of the seas by the east wind and broken, its mariners and cargo sinking — a literary type of the freighted vessel undone by wind that resonates with the Alexandrian grain ship overwhelmed here. Verbal contact is minimal; the link is thematic.

'Thou breakest the ships of Tarshish with an east wind' supplies a compact scriptural image of a great fleet-vessel shattered by an east wind, matching Euroclydon (the east-northeast gale). A brief, low-volume motif echo rather than a developed allusion.

The angel's nocturnal 'Don't be afraid' to Paul echoes the formula of the divine reassurance oracle that recurs across the OT, of which God's night-word to Abram ('Fear not... I am thy shield') is the paradigm. The salvation-oracle form (night setting, fear-not, promise of protection and destiny) is well attested; the specific verbal tie is to the formula, not this verse alone.

Isaiah's 'Fear not... when thou passest through the waters, I will be with thee; and through the rivers, they shall not overflow thee' fuses the fear-not oracle with the motif of preservation through the deep — exactly Paul's situation: assured deliverance through the storm, with no loss of life. The combination of formula and water-rescue gives this strong thematic coherence.

An angelic night visitation that opens with 'Fear not, Daniel' and conveys a divine message of assurance furnishes a close formal parallel to the angel standing by Paul at night saying 'Don't be afraid.' The angelophany-plus-reassurance pattern matches; verbal overlap is the shared fear-not formula.

Paul's confident promise that all aboard will be preserved anticipates the psalm's resolution — the distressed cry, God stilling the storm, and the survivors brought safe to harbor. The assurance that 'it will be just as it has been spoken to me' embodies the providential rescue the psalm celebrates.

The mariners' nighttime effort to reach land — taking soundings, dropping anchors, and the sailors' attempt to escape in the boat — recalls Jonah's sailors rowing hard to bring the ship to shore against the storm. A faint narrative resonance of seamen straining toward land amid tempest; little verbal contact.

Paul's pledge that 'not a hair will perish from any of your heads' reproduces the OT idiom of total preservation — Israel's oath over Jonathan that 'there shall not one hair of his head fall to the ground' — used to guarantee that no life will be lost. The proverbial formula is distinctive and its sense (life entirely safeguarded) is exactly Paul's.

The same hyperbole of inviolable safety — 'there shall not one hair of thy son fall to the earth' — secured by oath; an alternate locus for the 'not a hair shall perish' assurance Paul gives. Offered as a parallel attestation of the idiom.

Paul's taking bread, giving thanks to God before all, breaking and eating it draws on the OT practice of blessing God over food — 'thou shalt eat and be full, and thou shalt bless the LORD thy God.' The act of thanksgiving over bread before a meal coheres with this command, though here it is a custom evoked rather than a text cited.

The chapter's denouement realizes the psalm's climax: after the tempest, God 'bringeth them unto their desired haven' — here all 276 aboard 'escaped safely to the land.' The bringing of every imperiled person out of the storm to dry land is the psalmist's pattern of deliverance enacted in narrative.

Jonah's storm ends with the sea ceasing from its raging and the ship's company spared; likewise the wreck resolves with the violent sea finally beaching the vessel and every soul brought through alive. A typological resonance of storm-to-rescue, with the righteous man's presence proving the means of others' preservation.
